prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how reallocation across firms shapes who exports and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for B005 with Melitz and Helpman. My reasoning has shifted somewhat. Melitz (2003) is a clear originating model. It makes selection into exporting and reallocation across firms an explicit source of aggregate gains from trade. Helpman's credit rests on the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple analysis of exporting versus FDI with heterogeneous firms, and on related work linking firm selection to the pattern of bilateral trade flows. That credit does not depend on the monopolistic-competition base covered by Krugman's 2008 prize, and it does not depend on the protection-for-sale work in B020. The framework is more than twenty years old. Its central predictions about exporter selection and reallocation have been confronted with firm-level and transaction-level data in many countries, and it is now the standard way trade is modelled and measured. I weight work that has survived this kind of micro-data testing. My ranking of B011 against B005 is close, and I now see it as a judgment about how directly each result has been tested. I do not see it as a gap in quality. I also hold the narrow wording the chair asked about. The citation honours the theory of firm heterogeneity and selection and its welfare implications. It does not honour the empirical discovery of exporter-premium facts, which belongs to Bernard, Jensen and co-authors, and it does not honour the Ricardian Eaton-Kortum strand.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the main weakness. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions and are not credited on this entry, so a two-name award does not allocate all the credit in the field. Krugman's 2008 prize covers the earlier monopolistic-competition framework, so Helpman's marginal credit has to be argued from the heterogeneous-firm extensions. Some welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand, although the selection mechanism itself is robust. A committee could also reasonably judge that trade was adequately recognised in 2008. Finally, B011 has the narrowest and cleanest credit line on the shortlist (one 1997 paper, two authors). The opening discussion produced six preferred-part positions for it, which meets the vote threshold. I do not treat that count as evidence of merit, and I do not treat it as evidence against B011 either.

responses.point: Hassler holds that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clean two-author originators of the collateral-price feedback mechanism. He argues that the 2022 prize covered distinct ground (banks and financial crises), that the mechanism has been extended and used for nearly three decades, and that the committee can recognise a mechanism whose empirical size is not pinned down.
responses.response: Your framing has changed my view on one point. In round 1 I said the 2022 overlap weighed heavily with me. I now think that was overstated. Bank runs and bank-specific information frictions differ from dynamic amplification through collateral values in the real economy, and the overlap is mostly a citation-wording issue. I keep the identification difference. A prize can honour a mechanism that is established as a modelling building block, as you say, but I still weigh a long record of direct micro-data testing more heavily, and B005 has that record. If the committee wants a two-name B011 with a citation that separates collateral-price feedback from bank-focused and accelerator work, I would regard it as a serious and defensible prize, and it is my first alternative. I would not call it scientifically inferior to B005.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first, anchors the citation on selection and reallocation rather than the empirical exporter-premium facts, and raises a Melitz-centred credit as an option. He would not widen the group to Bernard or Eaton-Kortum, nor add Redding.
responses.response: I agree on wording and on not widening the group, which would turn a fairly clean credit into an allocation of a diffuse literature. On the chair's question about a Melitz-centred option, I still prefer the pair. Melitz alone would be defensible for the 2003 model. But Helpman's independent contribution is the export-versus-FDI analysis with heterogeneous firms and the work tying firm selection to bilateral trade patterns. Those are extensions that changed how the framework is used, and a Melitz-only award would understate them. I accept that the Krugman 2008 overlap makes the Helpman half harder to argue than the Melitz half. That is a real asymmetry, and the citation should not pretend otherwise. If the committee thought the pair could not be defended, a Melitz-only award would be preferable to adding names.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B011 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only, and names B005 as his first alternative. He sees the two as close and says that if the 2022 overlap proves decisive against B011, B005 is where he would go. His main criticism of B005 is that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited and that Krugman's prize covers adjacent ground.
responses.response: I agree the two cases are close, and I take your attribution point as the strongest argument against my configuration. I think it is manageable through wording. The citation names the theory of firm heterogeneity and selection, and it does not claim the whole empirical firm-trade literature. I do not think it is as clean as B011's credit line, and I will not claim it is. I also take your point on B019. My own opening first choice fails on attribution. Eight names and a three-person cap mean any trio omits decisive contributors, and I have not found a selection that fixes this, so B019 stays set aside. On your 'about 15 possible prizes' tournament framing, I cannot judge whether breadth of support or concentration of first places should matter. Neither tells me about merit, so I leave it aside.

responses.point: Andersson answered my B011 reservations in two parts: the 2022 prize concerned banks, while Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral and asset-price feedback in the real economy, and B019's eight names make it a worse fit for a prize that must name specific people. He treats B005 as a strong candidate, but ranks B011 higher on attribution.
responses.response: Your first point has moved me, as I note to Hassler above. The 2022 distinction is real, and it removes much of my overlap objection. Your second point on B019 I already conceded in round 1. The remaining difference between us is whether cleaner two-author attribution outweighs more direct empirical confirmation. I think that is a legitimate judgment call. I note you rank B005 as your first alternative, and I rank B011 as mine. If attribution care is the deciding criterion, B011 has the advantage. If testing against micro data is the deciding criterion, B005 does. I have not seen evidence that settles which criterion the committee should give priority.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can word a B005 citation that credits the theory of firm heterogeneity and selection without overreaching on Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.

How much of Helpman's credit is independent of Krugman's 2008 prize and of his separate B020 entry. I rely on general knowledge of the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple and related work, and I have not independently verified sources.

Whether the narrower B011 credit line (two names, one 1997 paper) should count for more than the more direct micro-data testing of B005. I do not think the evidence on the committee's criteria settles this.
How large the collateral-channel amplification is empirically. I have reduced my weight on the 2022 overlap but not on this identification question.
Whether the welfare conclusions of the B005 framework survive alternative functional forms. The selection mechanism looks robust, but the size of the gains appears structure-dependent.
A two-part configuration under the three-person cap: I have not found one that avoids weakening a clean credit line, so I keep a single part.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile with respect to Melitz, Helpman or the other credited names on B005, B011 and B012. My listed co-authors (Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom, Oosterbeek, van Ours) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. I was at Stockholm University from 2010 to 2017. That is an institutional overlap with the IIES group, including fellow members Hassler and Krusell, and it is not a link to a candidate. The profile does not tell me whether any B012 candidate has IIES ties, so I note that as an unknown. B012 is only an alternative in my configuration. In round 1 I referred to a remark attributed to Per Strömberg about Persson's past committee role. The chair reports that this remark does not appear in Strömberg's round-1 file, and I cannot verify it, so I withdraw any reliance on it. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
